subsubtopic: CANADA-U.S. AUTO PACT-EQUITABLE SHARING OF BENEFITS- MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising out of reports yesterday that the federal government has decided to subsidize the construction of two new auto parts plants by General Motors Limited and Ford Motors Limited to the tune of $116 million.
In light of the fact that the auto pact signed by Canada and the United States in 1965 commits both countries to policies that would allow the industry on both sides of the border to "participate on a fair and equitable basis in the expanding total market of both countries", I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce be instructed to reopen talks with the major auto makers in order to impress upon them the view that a level of investment consistent with our share of the North American automobile market is a legal and moral obligation on the part of the auto makers; that he be instructed to demand from them, within six months, plans as to how they intend to meet this quota of investment every year between now and 1985; and, finally, that he be instructed to refuse any requests for assistance from the auto makers in the form of grants or subsidies until they have presented satisfactory plans for meeting their target levels of investment and jobs in line with the Canadian share of the over-all North American automobile market.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR IMMEDIATE DISSOLUTION OF PARLIAMENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an urgent matter concerning the recent, obvious fact that the government and parliament are no longer running the country, which is now in the hands of an unholy triumvirate, the Gallup poll, the Goldfarb poll and Senator Keith Davey. I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie):
That the House deplores the failure of the government to deal with unemployment, inflation and the fallen dollar, that the House condemns the Prime Minister for withholding, up to now, an election from the Canadian people whereby they can pass judgment on this situation and, finally, that the Prime Minister request dissolution of the House by the Governor General immediately, in order to permit democracy to function and to dispel the widespread idea that the Liberal party colour has turned from red to yellow.

subsubtopic: STUDENT SUMMER EMPLOYMENT SURVEY-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing business. During the summer of 1976, the government, in an attempt to conceal the poor performance of its summer job-creation program, cancelled the summer student employment survey. Through public pressure, it was forced to reinstitute this survey in 1977.
Now that the summer of 1978 is almost upon us and university and secondary school students are about to enter the labour market, we find that the government has again discontinued the student summer employment survey, as a result of which student summer employment will no longer be reported by Statistics Canada. Since this will make long-range planning impossible for both the private and public sectors, I would move, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt):
That the government stop playing games with the future of Canada's young people, undertake to be forthright in the reporting of student unemployment, and stop trying to hide its job-creation failures by deleting reports; and further, that the student summer employment survey be conducted through the summer of 1978.

subsubtopic: POLICING OF FISHING QUOTAS WITHIN 200-MILE LIMIT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. In light of the open and apparent disagreements and conflicts in policy which have been so evident over the past few months between the federal Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, provincial premiers and provincial fisheries ministers, can the federal minister indicate whether there has been some reconciliation of views or a common approach to the very serious problems affecting our east and west coast fishermen, and can he indicate whether there has been a final solution to the inadequate policing and surveillance of fishing quotas which presently exist within the 200-mile limit?

speakeroldname: Hon. Rom6o LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: POLICING OF FISHING QUOTAS WITHIN 200-MILE LIMIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the consultations we had with provincial ministers in December and February there was general agreement as to the policy direction which should be taken. I recognize that provincial ministers will differ in degree with some of the policies we are putting forward, but the fact remains-I have indicated this before-that I cannot delegate and, in fact, the constitution as it is presently written does not allow me to delegate the final authority for management of the fisheries.
On the second question raised by the hon. member, there have been reported acts of violation. Legal advice is being sought as to whether identification of fishing vessels' locations by plane will stand up in court. If they will, violators will be taken to court.

federal government as it relates to freezer trawlers may at least be examined and, hopefully, altered?

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the hon. member does not know it, but this is the second year in which there has been a fishing plan for the whole Atlantic region. The fishing plan is working astonishingly well, with regions and quotas reserved both for inshore and for offshore. This, of course, is subject to consultation with representatives of the industry, processors and fishermen, provincial governments and those who have an interest in the subject.
With regard to the second question, I have before me no applications for licensing of freezer trawlers which would take species like capelin, hake, grenadier or argentine. All the applications I have for licences-although they do mention these species in the first paragraph of the letter-always seek access to red fish, flat fish or northern cod. I have indicated very clearly that the present fleet has the capacity to catch the stocks which are available to Canada, which are over 80 per cent for 1979 and 76 per cent for 1978. The problem is not one of expansion; it is one of increasing the catch rate of the vessels which are just now becoming economical.

speechtext: In view of the deterioration in the situation of west coast fisheries, particularly in light of the injunction which was issued last week, will the minister tell us what positive steps he has taken to ensure that the Canadian viewpoint is given a good hearing during the injunction proceedings before the U.S. courts?

subtopic: CANADA-U.S. DISPUTE ON WEST COAST FISHERIES
speechtext: In light of the one-week delay in the imposition of the injunction, has the minister any special words of comfort to issue to the fishermen as they set out this weekend for the salmon fishing grounds, so that they may know with assurance that they will be able to go into those grounds freely and fish under the terms of the interim agreement? REQUEST PRIME MINISTER PERSONALLY INTERVENE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER RESPECTING DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the right hon. Prime Minister arising out of the hardship which may be imposed on British Columbia fishermen by the ban which has been imposed by the court in the United States with respect to Canadian fishermen operating in U.S. coastal waters.
I ask the Prime Minister if he would personally intervene with President Carter so that, if the ban is upheld, the U.S. government would undertake not to enforce it until such time as the two negotiators for Canada and the United States are able to work out a temporary agreement pending ratification of the Canadian-American fisheries agreement.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REQUEST PRIME MINISTER PERSONALLY INTERVENE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER RESPECTING DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to remind the hon. member that it was as a result of my representations to President Carter a little more than a
May 10, 1978

year ago, assisted by the Minister of Fisheries, that we obtained this interim agreement.
I should also like to remind him that the form in which his question was put is not correct, in the sense that there has not been a ban. There is a question of a ban, an injunction, before the courts now and, as the Minister of Fisheries reminded the House, President Carter's administration is fighting against this injunction. Surely that indicates that President Carter is not only aware of what Canada told him last year through the minister and myself, but is fighting to uphold the message that both of us agreed to last year. Regarding the rest of the question, the hon. member will recall that in its very form it was hypothetical.

subtopic: REQUEST PRIME MINISTER PERSONALLY INTERVENE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER RESPECTING DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the fact that the proposed temporary agreement has not been ratified by the United States Congress, there is every likelihood that the prohibition on Canadian fishermen will be upheld by the courts.
In view of the fact that Monday, May 15, is the opening of the halibut season, and that the fisheries' representative on the Pacific coast has informed already British Columbia fishermen that they should plan to continue their fishing off the Alaska coast, and I am sure the Prime Minister recognizes what could happen if there were confrontations, does he not think it is sufficiently important to take it up with the American government, so that we do not have a situation wherein British Columbia fishermen are intercepted off the Alaskan coast in the event that the prohibition and the injunction are sustained in the course of the next few days?

subtopic: REQUEST PRIME MINISTER PERSONALLY INTERVENE WITH PRESIDENT CARTER RESPECTING DISPUTE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am afraid, once again, the question indicates that the hon. member is misinformed. He suggests that I take something up with the American government. Therefore, it is of little avail to suggest that I take it up with the American government: they are on our side and they are acting in a sense for us.
The hon. member has suggested the difficulty: it is that Congress itself has not passed this agreement. But the administration is doing its best to get it passed. I do not think the hon. member would suggest that I could tell Congress what it should be doing. Neither do I agree with the hon. member when he predicts what the courts will decide. If the courts go against us, Your Honour will realize that we are in an hypothesis here and the question is hypothetical. Let me just remind the hon. member what our government, and particularly the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, did last year when we had to apply pressure on the Americans. We banned some of their fishing in our waters.
One does not like to talk like this, because we are hoping Congress will see where justice lies in this question. Perhaps the hon. member is unintentionally provoking the government

into making some retaliatory threats before even the cause for such threats has become evident. So I suggest this line of questioning is not appropriate.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION MEASURES BE ADOPTED TO IMPROVE INDUSTRY CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct a question to the Minister of Fisheries. I am sure the minister is aware of the feelings of hostility by some fishermen toward the imposition of regulations that seriously affect their livelihood, without what they consider proper consultation.
Is the minister considering a directive or a general investigation to see what can be done to improve relations, not only between his department and fishermen but to co-ordinate policy among federal and provincial ministries so that inshore fishermen can be given better bait-freezing and storage facilities, improved slipways and things like this which are required to improve conditions in the industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. Rom6o LeBlanc (Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
subsubtopic: SUGGESTION MEASURES BE ADOPTED TO IMPROVE INDUSTRY CONDITIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where the federal government is responsible in the case, for example, of the management of stocks, changes in the conditions of access to stocks, licensing, etc., obviously we have a very high level of consultation. In fact, I decentralized, not only to Halifax as a region and to St. John's but to area managers in places like Sydney, northern New Brunswick, etc., a fair level of authority so local problems can be dealt with by local officials in co-operation with local fishermen. I also instituted a program whereby 20 community service officers of the Department of Fisheries have the responsibility of constantly being in touch with the fishermen.
Obviously, there are times when decisions have to be made, for conservation reasons, where no level of consultation will produce agreement and at one point you simply cannot delegate the final decision to anyone. In the area of federal-provincial co-operation, it is obvious that, for example in respect of both subsidies and other programs, they are synchronized with programs such as the fishermen's loan boards of the provincial governments.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTION MEASURES BE ADOPTED TO IMPROVE INDUSTRY CONDITIONS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer and I ask him, with respect-while most fishermen, I believe, will concede he has their best interests at heart-will he not take a look at the attitude that prevails among scallop fishermen, people who are concerned with aquaculture, for example, and people very much concerned that there is no sensitivity shown to setting proper seasons for scallop fishing, for example, in Nova Scotia, in order that he can be satisfied that his officials, the people he has appointed, are really doing their job in consulting with and getting the benefit of the experience the industry has? speechtext:
If I might continue, Mr. Speaker. I spoke in Thompson, Manitoba, on Friday, April 7. Not being a Liberal, I did not have a script. I spoke off the cuff for 40 minutes. That speech was reported in the Winnipeg Free Press of April 11, four days later. There was a small report. I need to refer to that to show how this canard got started. It is being used by the NDP outside this House, and now inside.
In that report in the Winnipeg Free Press it states that I said that a federal Progressive Conservative government would make, and I quote:

Privilege-Mr. Crosbie
-"Premier Sterling Lyon look like a pussycat" in cutting back on excessive civil servants,-
It adds that I told the federal PC meeting for Churchill that "Joe Clark's government would trim 60,000 civil servants by attrition". I never mentioned 60,000; I never mentioned 100; I never mentioned one civil servant being cut, in the speech.
I wrote the Winnipeg Free Press on April 19 telling them that their account was inaccurate, and telling them what I did say. What I did say was that the Conservative party would free the private sector from unnecessary regulation, restrain the growth of government expenditure, restrain the growth of government public servants and that we meant what we said, not like the Liberals, and that in that direction we would make Sterling Lyon look like a pussycat. Nothing was mentioned about laying off any civil servants.
On April 25 I sent a copy of that letter to the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) because 1 knew he was going to prevaricate around the country with this statement. I already had a tipoff on that. Therefore I sent the Leader of the NDP a copy of my letter to the Free Press. It was published in the Winnipeg Free Press on April 26.
Next, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby, the Leader of the NDP, used it outside the House. Now the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond changes even what I was supposed to have said by the Winnipeg Free Press, stating that I said that 60,000 public servants will be laid off. That is a libel on a member, in my opinion. As Mark Twain said, "A lie can travel half way around the world while the truth is putting on its shoes." While I am putting on my shoes, this lie is travelling around the world.

The present Conservative member of the federal parliament for Churchill, Cecil Smith, was visibly uncomfortable during his own nomination meeting when John Crosbie of Newfoundland promised that the next federal Conservative government would make Sterling Lyon "took like a pussycat" in reducing the size of the civil service. Crosbie said Joe Clark would cut 60,000 federal jobs.

The hon. member says he did not say it, and he says he has nothing in writing. I was told by their members to see what he had in writing, but he was not here yesterday, so I raised the matter largely because I did not think we should be talking like this when there are one million unemployed in this country. People from the Atlantic region should be talking about decentralizing the bureaucracy, not cutting people off from it.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to inform the House that it is the intention of the government to introduce legislation to increase the basic rate of pensions for disabled veterans by $310.76 annually to $7,471.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PENSION INCREASES FOR DISABLED VETERANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF PENSION INCREASES FOR DISABLED VETERANS
speechtext:
The proposed increase is in addition to the automatic increase provided under the Pension Act each January in accordance with the consumer price index.
This increase is significant at a time when, as all Canadians recognize, government expenditures must be restrained, and it demonstrates the government's determination to honour a long-standing commitment to ensure an adequate income to disabled veterans and their dependents in recognition of the service they have rendered to their country. The enabling legislation will be introduced as soon as possible to make the increase effective July 1, and will provide for proportionate increases with respect to lesser disabilities and related pensions. Similar appropriate increases will be provided to those who qualify for prisoner of war compensation.
I am sure all hon. members will co-operate to ensure that this legislation receives quick passage.

May 10, 1978
Railway Act

The House resumed, from Monday, May 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Abbott (for Mr. Lang) that Bill C-17, to amend the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act and the Railway Act and to amend and repeal certain other statutes in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass, and of the amendment (Mr. Murta) (p. 5176).

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to participate again in the debate on Bill C-17, the CNR refinancing bill, as it is known. I also want to support the amendment moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta). I spoke during second reading debate for the purpose of making known some of my views on this CNR refinancing and also on the Hall commission and on railway abandonment in my home province of Manitoba. A little later I would like to add to some of those earlier remarks.
As hon. members know, our party intends to vote against this bill. Our reasons for not supporting Bill C-17 have been put on the record by other members of the Progressive Conservative party. We do not feel that this bill serves any real purpose. The government has tried to make it appear as if the passage of this bill will save Canadian taxpayers money, but a close examination shows that this is merely an illusion, a stage trick.
The CNR's own profit projections for the next five years show that the capital restructuring provided in this bill is not necessary for the corporation to make a profit. The first quarter of this year has produced a healthy profit for the railway, and its own projections show that this is going to be the case for the next few years whether this bill is passed or not. With this bill the profits will be only that much greater.
CN is a Crown corporation, and therefore its shareholders are the citizens of Canada. Under our democratic parliamentary system we are the peoples' representatives, and therefore CN is accountable first and foremost to parliament and not to the capital market. The problem, however, is how to make CN accountable to parliament.
As hon. members are aware, there is at present another royal commission in existence apart from the McDonald commission which is getting so much publicity, namely, the commission on corporate concentration, which will shortly hand down its recommendations on the basis of which the government has promised to prepare its legislation governing Crown corporations. We think that the bill before us should be deferred until that time.
The last time that CNR came before parliament asking to be relieved of its debts was in 1952 when the railway began a huge program of capital expenditures, and less than a decade

later, in 1961, generated a debt of slightly under $1 billion. But despite all the expenditures, CN transportation service began to decline after that. The CN became involved in many other ventures, but CN railway transport has not improved at all in the 26 years since 1952.
We in the Conservative party believe that now is not the time to give passage to Bill C-17. There are just too many questions hanging over the future of rail service in this country. The government has committed itself to a large expenditure in order to upgrade the grain handling lines in western Canada. There may be an adjustment of the Crow rates- something which I personally fear-but that is uncertain, and I am not reassured by the odd noises from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to the effect that there will be no tampering with the Crow rates. However, that is another subject.
Also, CN has been relieved of what is perhaps its biggest burden, that is, the rail passenger service, with the formation of VIA Rail, but no one really knows yet whether VIA Rail will prove to be a wise decision or a big mistake. Personally I support VIA Rail but the experience in the United States with Amtrak, in a country with a much larger travelling public to support such a venture, has brought a mixed reaction. I wonder what our experience in Canada will be. In light of these uncertainties, we believe that this is not the time to consider Bill C-17 and that it would be more sensible to defer it until these various uncertainties have been cleared away.
Now I would like to make some comments about a subject that is of great concern to me and to my constituents, that is, railway abandonment. It continues to be a very hot topic in Manitoba, particularly in my constituency where there are so many branch lines. Perhaps the reason is that, according to the Hall commission, the province of Manitoba was the province most "overbuilt" with railways during the great period of railway expansion in Canada from about 1880 to 1920. The result is that today there is a multitude of branch lines in the province which are concentrated in the narrow southern quarter of Manitoba. Most of these lines are not economical and some have already been abandoned, or will be soon.
In the central Interlake region of my constituency there is an 80 mile long CNR branch line which is known as the Inwood subdivision. The grain receiving points on this line are three Manitoba pool elevators, one at Broad Valley, and two at Fisher Branch. The Fisher Branch facilities were expanded not too long ago. The amount of grain handled by these three elevators fluctuates, depending on the type of crop year in that region. As of March 1 of this year, the three elevators at Fisher Branch and Broad Valley together handled a total of 8,585 metric tonnes of grain. In other words, this is what the Inwood line handled in the first three months of this year.
The Hall commission recommended that this line be abandoned. I am against the abandonment of this line, and I have always been. I want that clearly understood. I have argued for the retention of this line as part of the basic rail network on many occasions. However, the Hall commission recommended its abandonment, in spite of my representations as well as
May 10, 1978

those of many others, of course, made to Mr. Justice Hall and to the other commissioners.
For the Inwood line, the Hall commission made a unique recommendation. It suggested that the two elevators at Fisher Branch be retained in service on the abandoned line as off-line loaders and that farmers continue to deliver to Fisher Branch. From Fisher Branch the grain would be trucked by commercial truck to the CP's Arborg railhead, which is about 20 miles distant. This off-line loading experiment has not been instituted by this government, and may never be. However, I have a great many reservations about the practicality of such an operation.
In the Interlake there are four branch lines. Of these, the Inwood line is the only one which is not paralleled by a paved provincial trunk highway along most of its length. There is some pavement in the north, but it is not parallel to the Inwood line. The roads are all low grade. The Inwood subdivision is in the very special position of being the primary mode of transportation in most of the area which it serves.
The principal commodity moved over this line is, of course, grain, but there is some other traffic as well. Grain makes up about 85 per cent of the total, pulpwood makes up 7 per cent, and the other 8 per cent is made up by coal, fertilizer, lumber, and farm implements and machinery. For the grain traffic, the Hall commission recommended the off-line concept. I must admit that I would be very interested to observe such an experiment in operation but, for all that I know of this region, it is not really an answer to the grain handling problems of the Interlake.
The biggest single reason that such an operation is neither practical nor viable is that the roads in the area are completely inadequate for large capacity grain trucks. The Inwood line runs through two of the three local government districts, or LGDs, in the Interlake, Fisher and Armstrong. These LGDs do not have the resource tax base to undertake the road development and upgrading which would be required for heavy hauling by truck. It is not only the expense of truck hauling, and which would be very great in any case, which is involved. There is also the consideration that trucking is an inefficient and fuel-wasteful means of transport as compared with the diesel locomotive which the experts variously estimate to be 18 times more efficient than the gasoline powered truck, based on ton capacity and fuel consumption.
In all of Canada only about 8 per cent of the total land is farm land, and this is declining every year. However, this is not true of the Interlake. If hon. members want to see a real frontier where raw virgin land is still being broken by the plough, they should visit the north central Interlake area of Manitoba in my constituency.
In the Dallas-Red Rose area Canada's arable farm land is being developed at present. This is in contrast to what is happening in most other parts of the country where agricultural land is disappearing. This is only possible in that part of the province of Manitoba because of the existence of the Inwood rail line. Even so, the local delivery point for these new farms now is Fisher Branch, which is more than 40 miles away for
Railway Act
many of the producers. However, the off-line concept would involve a further haulage by truck from Fisher Branch to CP's Arborg railhead, a further 30 miles or so. Of course, this would make the new farms in the Dallas-Red Rose region completely uneconomic. It is clear that closure of the Inwood subdivision would effectively halt agricultural expansion in the north central Interlake.
When I last spoke in the House on March 2 about the problems of rail transportation in the Interlake, and about the Hall commission's recommendations for the Inwood line, I believe I stated that the farmers of the area wanted the commission's off-line experiment for Fisher Branch to be undertaken. The farmers have told me, however, that this is decidedly not the case. Naturally they do not want to lose their Inwood line, any more than I do. We are not against the experiment, but we do not want to lose our railway for the sake of it.
I should like to quote from a letter which I received a short time ago from the president of the Fisher Branch and District Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Tom Magnusson. I believe it sums up very well how the grain producers of the Interlake feel about the Inwood subdivision. In part the letter reads as follows:
... In our investigations locally, the farmers do not feel that the off-line elevator concept is indeed the most economical in the long term, nor even feasible, given the present infrastructure and circumstances. The Fisher Branch and District Chamber of Commerce takes the following position in support of our local farmers: (1) that rail service must be maintained to Fisher Branch through either (A) continuance of the present line and the upgrading of same, or (B) construction of a spur line from Fisher Branch-Broad Valley area to either the CPR Arborg line or the CNR along provincial trunk highway number 6; or (2) should the off-line elevator concept be instituted, that the CNR Inwood subdivision be left intact and maintained until the success and feasibility of the trucking operation to Arborg be determined. This would allow the CTC to reverse its decision if the trucking operation is not successful.
My position is exactly the same. It is the only way in which I would support the Hall recommendation. Mr. Magnusson's letter continues:
You will likely be aware of why our farmers have taken this stand. I would point out, however, that the data the Hall commission based its recommendations on is not without challenge and therefore the recommendations should not be etched in stone. In fact our information is that the Prairie Rail Action Committee has commissioned another study on the cost factors involved in this "off-line elevator" recommendation. Also, our last year's crop indicates that we indeed have a much greater production potential than the 750,000 bushel handle used by the Hall commission as the basis of their recommendation.
On many occasions the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that he believes that in Canada today nothing is carved in stone-not the constitutional arrangements, not federal-provincial relations, not anything. He is very flexible and willing to negotiate anything except outright separatism. Members of the Conservative party are not entirely convinced that all things are negotiable. However, in view of the government's stated willingness to be amiable and flexible, perhaps the Minister of Transport will re-examine the matter of the Inwood line and the recommendations of the Hall commission. Certainly there are extenuating circumstances here. In any case, the recommendations of the commission are now two

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
years out of date. I urge the Minister of Transport to re-examine the entire question of the future of the Inwood subdivision.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to make brief comments on the bill now under consideration.
The primary objective of Bill C-17 is to allow the CN to proceed with recapitalization. The conversion of the $800 million debt in no par value capital stock will allow the CN to reimburse the treasury through dividends on its earnings instead of being compelled, mostly in theory it must be added, to repay its debt. Considering that the CN balance sheet has shown profits for the past two years, that fact seriously prompts us to pass the bill. We would thus show our confidence in the management of that Crown corporation. In light of those factors, I feel that the bill is constructive. On the other hand, as a member of the opposition it is my duty to point out some dangers of giving carte blanche to the CN.
One of the indirect and no less significant results of the adoption of this bill would be to place the Crown corporation in a favourable position to borrow funds on money markets. This is not bad in itself, for everything would depend on the final use of these funds. If these funds are to be used to improve the railway system, make it more practical both for travellers and shippers, that is to serve the Canadian public better, this indirect result is desirable. On the other hand, if these funds are earmarked for investments in areas which are not consistent with the traditional vocation of the CN, I am against it. The CN is not an industrial and commercial holding company but a public utility. Its first function is to transport people and merchandise to destination, and to do so economically, whenever possible. It is a fact that there are circumstances where we cannot have both effectiveness and profitability. Under such circumstances, the service to the public must prevail over profitability, at least within certain limits. In fact, the CN is a Crown corporation because it is a recognized public utility. I feel many hon. members in this House would like to know more about the CN's medium and long-term plans in light of this possibility of getting new funds.
I know that several of my western colleagues are not satisfied with the CN performance in their region. On the other hand I would not like them to feel that everything is perfect in the east. If western shippers cannot find cars to ship grains, there is a similar problem in the east in relation with the lumber industry. Many lumber companies cannot get the cars they need to ship sawed lumber to American markets. Those companies are faced with the impossibility of meeting their delivery schedule and are therefore losing many new contracts. The problem does not stem from the employees' slow productivity or lack of leadership by the management which made efforts to get those contracts abroad. Everyone knows that the

government likes to use both those excuses to hide its negligence. No, in this case it is the lack of foresight by the Canadian National which is clearly responsible for those lost contracts.
I was saying the CN must not launch into all sorts of investment which are not within its field of competence. To this I would add that the CN will have to be monitored closely even for some investments which may be within its field of competence. A related example which comes to mind is the proposed acquisition of Nordair by Air Canada. Although by doing so Air Canada would stay in its particular area of competence, it is not at all certain this transaction would be to the advantage of travellers and Canadians in general. On the other hand, whoever cares to open his eyes will see clearly that this transaction would severely limit the possibilities of expansion of another airline, namely Quebecair. I do not think a Crown corporation should have the right to take advantage of some privileges that are peculiar to nationally owned corporations to harm privately owned corporations. That kind of abuse should never be allowed.
We will have to be on our guard and see to it that this kind of abuse does not happen in the CN. For this reason, I wish the government had taken advantage of the presentation of this legislation to introduce controls and the obligation for the CN to report on a more direct basis than it does now. I would not want this wish to be interpreted as a lack of confidence in CN management. On the opposite, as I said earlier those people are to be commended for their healthy Financial administration in the last few years. Indeed, the figures are revealing: in two years the CN went from a deficit of $16 million in 1975 to profits of $28 million in 1977. But if its record is so good, I do not see why the CN should be afraid of the right of representatives of the people to have some control and especially to ask some questions. We sometimes make a lot of noise in this House, but God knows that we are not so bad. After all, we are entitled to know about the operations of such an important company, a Crown corporation. It would be only normal for the elected representatives of the people to be better informed on the operations of this company.
Finally, I would like to suggest a possibility that I believe very progressive. Following passage of this bill, the CN will most probably decide to look for new capital on the money markets. According to tradition, these funds will come either from the Canadian market or, as is the case too often, from foreign markets. I believe that if the government really wanted to innovate and be progressive, it could consider allowing the Bank of Canada, which is the bank of all Canadians, to lend to the CN the funds it might need. Of course, the interest rate charged would be the minimum. Canadians should not exploit one another. It would be quite normal for them to co-operate.
Since the Bank of Canada belongs to the people, I think it would be quite normal for it to help a Crown corporation like the CN. Under the formula that I have suggested, the develop-
May 10, 1978

ment of the CN would benefit all Canadians and not only the bankers, whether Canadian or foreign. Moreover, this would allow better control over the development of the CN since the loans could include very specific conditions which would meet the needs of Canadians. Mr. Speaker, I believe that this suggestion should be considered very seriously and I hope that, in doing so, the government will be open-minded and even innovative.
I believe that the cabinet should review this bill so as to include the means of financing this utility that I have suggested, which would make it more acceptable. This is why I sincerely believe that consideration of this bill should be postponed for some time as suggested in the motion which has been moved to allow the cabinet to make the improvements that I have suggested.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it may be, as Gordie Lightfoot said, there was a time in this great land when the railroads did not run, but it seems that must have been a very long time ago. I am always amazed in looking back at some of our history, economical and political, to find since how many years railways have had almost a fatal fascination for politicians, perhaps even before they did for economists.
Railways in Canada, said Robert McQueen in the "Canadian Historical Review" back in 1936, are far from being an economic problem. He said, they are born of, nourished in, are and will continue to be a part of Canadian politics.
Back in 1851 that great Nova Scotian, Joseph Howe, in a speech in Quebec, said in respect of railways, when talking about the future of what was then the colonies in North America:
To the advocates of legislative union I say, your scheme is impracticable without the railroads.
He went on to say as well, on another occasion:
I am neither a prophet, nor the son of a prophet, yet I will venture to predict that in five years we shall make the journey hence to Quebec and Montreal and Home through Portland and St. John by rail;-
This is the part that fascinates me:
-and I believe that many in this room will live to hear the whistle of the stream-engine in the passes of the Rocky Mountains and to make the journey from Halifax to the Pacific in five or six days.
He said that in Halifax on May 15, 1851.
With 127 years or so having passed, we are still not able to get to the Pacific from the eastern coast in much less than five days by rail.
I suggest, when we look at this particular bill and the amendment that I am speaking on today, we should consider why the railways, despite the fact that many hundreds of millions of dollars have been written off capital indebtedness, have been so slow in many areas to adopt modern technology.
Railway Act
Since the war, for example, in the U.S.S.R., a country with climatic and geographical conditions resembling Canada, we have seen the electrification of literally thousands of miles of railway track. This point was made very strikingly by Professor J. Lukasiewicz, a well known Carleton University professor, who has written from time to time on both the modernization and the obsolescence of the Canadian railway system.
As members of parliament, and as Canadians, I think we should demand to know more from the top management of the major railways in this country why they have been so slow to adopt in trains what would appear to be fairly rudimentary technological advances. Now with the advent of VIA Rail, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) quite rightly is emphasizing that it would be to the advantage of all Canadians, for many reasons, to promote greater use of passenger facilities. Yet I do not understand why more has not been done to make the use of railways more attractive to businessmen and, indeed, to all types of commuters and passengers.
I believe it is possible in this day and age for railway passengers to be provided access to telephones so that businessmen, for example, who wished to make a trip from Montreal to Toronto or from Montreal to Halifax would be able to use the railway as sort of a mobile office, if they had reasonable access to radio or some other type of telephone communications.
The same is true, I suggest, of other technological advances that could be brought in to make the trains more attractive for a journey which is, of necessity, much longer than one has to endure by aircraft. Why should television not be available in some parts of the modern train? Why should there not be a rudimentary library available, and a more attractive and less expensive canteen service? All these things would do a great deal in a practical way to help encourage greater usage of the railways. This, of course, has to be the bottom line; if railways are not used by a greater percentage of travellers, then certainly they will not be profitable and we will continue to be the recipient of requests by the CNR to come in every once in a while and write off several hundreds of millions or, as one member said, "another great train robbery" at the expense of the taxpayers.
I think it is also pretty obvious that the benefits the legislation we are discussing today is supposed to provide, while superficially attractive, are not necessarily indicative of what will really happen. We are told that one of the main purposes of the bill is to convert approximately $800 million of debt owed the government by the CNR to equity. A lot of benefits are supposed to flow from this. We are supposed to eliminate the necessity of the federal government picking up deficits which occur from time to time.
We are supposed, as well, to improve the debt-equity ratio, as was done recently with our national air carrier, and it will also supposedly free the government from having to purchase 4 per cent of preferred shares at an annual cost to the government of $80 million, which supposedly is based upon 3 per cent of the gross revenues of the CN system. However, it was well documented before the committee that the governmemt was never obliged to purchase preferred shares of the CN from

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
1960 onwards. The government was compelled to purchase the shares only from 1952 to 1960 as stipulated in the 1952 recapitalization act. However, the statement that was first made in this House by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) some time ago, that the passing of Bill C-17 would be an automatic saving to the public of Canada because of the readjustment of the capital structure, is not at this time very self-evident. It places the bona fides of the entire bill under some suspicion.
As I understand it, the CNR has proven that it is going to make a modest profit in the next few years anyway whether this bill is passed or not. The projection for 1979 is a profit in excess of $60 million without Bill C-17. If it does become law the projection is for $136 million profit. By 1982, the profit, if Bill C-17 is not passed, is supposed to be in the vicinity of $140 million, whereas if it is passed the profit will be $267 million. This may be, however laudable the bottom line from the point of view of the accountant or economist, an excessive profit, taking into account that CN, like Air Canada, also has a primary duty to provide service as well as to make a profit. Ideally, of course, they have to do both, but to concentrate too much on the profit motive is not necessarily in the best interests of either the railway or the country.
Coming back to the object of the CNR and how, in the past, I feel in some ways it has been derelict in its duties, I would like to make a suggestion to the Minister of Transport, and to CN management as a whole, that greater emphasis be placed on carrying non-perishable commodities by rail. It is not only inefficient, as my colleague from Portage just pointed out, to carry some of these commodities by truck, but it is also energy wasting and very destructive to our highways. Pulp wood, particularly in the province of Nova Scotia, is one of the commodities that lends itself to being moved far more efficiently by rail. In doing this it would be more energy efficient, make our highways safer and less congested, and it would also be a much more satisfactory method for the industry.
However, herein lies another problem, Mr. Speaker. Car allocation by the CNR to do this, periodically presents a problem. It presents a problem in my constituency for many industries, but principally it presents a problem for pulp companies. Another problem that we find is that the CNR is not very aggressive in its attempts to go after new business, which is part and parcel of making railways profitable. Like most businesses, if you do not achieve a reasonable amount of volume you are not going to be able to achieve very much efficiency. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald in an editorial a few weeks ago commented, and they were speaking about the CNR at the time:
The railway has not made an impressive showing in seeking new business. One wonders, for example, how much better business might be on the south shore line (of N.S.) if as much energy has been poured into an aggressive marketing and service as was expended in trying to get permission for abandonment.
Assuming that the railways eventually gets the benefit of this recapitalization, and assuming that management have additional funds, either as a result of the capital they generate

in profits or as a result of the benefits which parliament may see fit to give them, surely they must undertake a comprehensive effort to purchase more railway rolling stock and to upgrade not only the quality and quantity of their cars- refrigeration cars, pulp cars, flatcars, and so on-but they have to do some more meaningful work on upgrading the roadbeds. It is literally possible between Halifax and Montreal, on some of the passenger trains, on the steep grades, to jump out of the car and run alongside the train for several hundred yards, and get back on again. I do not know whether or not this is a fault of the diesel engines that are pulling the train because they are under powered. I rather suspect it is as a result of the conditions of the roadbed in some areas, which make it very hazardous for these trains to achieve a reasonable amount of speed. When one examines the average speed of a passenger train in Canada, and I am relying on my memory for this and going back to something that Professor Lukasiewicz wrote, it is something around 35 miles an hour, which is a very painful contrast to the 500 miles an hour that one can achieve with most jet aircraft today.
Railways must also take a more human view and more direct interest in their customers and employees as well. As a member of parliament I have received representations from people who complain bitterly that the service reps and the railway management in general are not interested sometimes in providing cars for some of their seasonal and short-term needs. I would trust, in connection with this more or less general consideration of the future of the CN, that management will take a sweeping look at their sales promotion techniques as well as their labour-management techniques because, as I started to say a few moments ago, at times the shortage of railway rolling stock is exacerbated by the fact that many of the needed cars are kept in the United States and cannot be recalled to Canada during certain peak periods of usage when they are needed.
I am quite prepared to admit that I have a special interest in seeing the CNR purchase a reasonable amount of modern and much-needed rolling stock. In my constituency in Trenton, Nova Scotia, we have one of the most capable railway producing industries in Canada, or in the world for that matter. As I said publicly a few days ago, I want to express my appreciation to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) for keeping me informed, and for his encouragement in making certain that we recently had an order for railway rolling stock for the continent of Africa, and he indicated several other countries where we might expect further business. The Secretary of State for External Affairs went on to say at that time that one of the reasons that Canadian manufacturers in this area are able to compete internationally is because of the efficiency and capability of our domestic industry. I am particularly proud that we have an industry in Nova Scotia that, despite its geographic disadvantages, has proven over the years that it can produce a very fine product.
One of the obvious failures of Bill C-17, and one of the justifications for this particular amendment, is that it is not necessarily the time to pass this legislation until we see, for
May 10, 1978

example, what the Sullivan commission in Newfoundland is going to say, until we see how the activities of VIA Rail are going to be reflected throughout the system, and particularly because Bill C-17 does not appear to provide or strengthen accountability to parliament to any significant degree.
Coming back to the primary purpose of our national railway system, our transportation policy in general has always been based on competition where market forces are in play. There has been some vacillation in this regard over the years. The current Minister of Transport has brought forward a user-pay policy, and his predecessor had a different policy, in some cases there was no policy, and in some areas there may still be none, but by and large any transportation company of the size of CNR affects to a great extent the entire transportation network across the country.
It is fair comment to say, and it may have been said already, and perhaps the CPR has said something about this as well that the CPR has been very, very quiet on this particular bill, and I am wondering why that is. Do they see it as a forerunner to the nationalization of the CPR? It is no secret that CPR in recent years would have been very pleased to get out of the transportation business.
For several reasons, some of them have been stated by previous speakers and some I have enumerated today, it will do no harm and it will provide a better opportunity to assess the whole situation with regard to our national railway system if this particular piece of legislation is given a six-months' hoist and not passed at this time. There is no particular need at this time for this bill to be passed. Therefore I am pleased to speak in support of the amendment of the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on the amendment standing in the name of my colleague, the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), regarding Bill C-17, an act to recapitalize the CNR.
I am far from being the oldest member of this House and yet I can remember in my lifetime-and I do not mind saying I am under 34 years of age-of going up to what we called the "tank" in Shelburne, Nova Scotia. Literally it was a tank on a tower by Blacks Brook. Anyone from the south shore of Nova Scotia will certainly know where Blacks Brook is. Once or twice a day the steam engines would come up to the tank at Blacks Brook and fill up, and I used to watch them. So, in my lifetime we have changed from that kind of locomotion in the rail industry to the modern diesels.
I can remember the first day when a diesel came down the tracks into Shelburne and the whole town turned out. It was a great spectacle to see what a diesel engine looked like. That is all in my short lifetime.
I am in support of the amendment that will hoist this legislation for some six months primarily because of what the bill and what the government have not done. Here it is, May 10, 1978, and we are in the House of Commons without
Railway Act
legislation regarding rail transportation within our cities-I am talking about modern rapid transit systems-despite the promises made some four years ago during the election campaign of 1974 by this government. I have a copy of those promises. I see the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) is in the House. I know that this government hoped that these election promises had been lost. But not so, sir. I diligently kept them over the years. Later on I will read them to this government and ministers can hear what they promised to do for rail transportation in this country.
Why should this bill not contain matters relevant to rapid transit systems? There are several reasons. Our major centres in Canada are centres of consumption. We know that right now some 65 per cent of Canadians live in urban centres. In another ten to 12 years, at least by 1990, 90 per cent of Canadians will live in urban centres, and yet today we do not have in place in Canada a strategy for rapid transit systems for our major centres. I am speaking of Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver, at least those three cities, if not others.
We know as well that this country is facing an oil gap. Prior to 1975 the term "oil gap" was unheard of. It was not in the vocabulary of Canadians. We know that at the moment half of the energy consumed in Canada in terms of oil and gas is in intra-city transportation. By the projections of the National Energy Board, and I am somewhat alarmed as other Canadians are that these projections change from time to time, their last projection showed that we will be facing a critical shortage of energy within the next 15 to 20 years. This means that Canada will import offshore oil in an amount of around 25 per cent to 30 per cent of our needs.
If we could put into place in our large urban centres, which will house 90 per cent of Canadians in another decade, mass rapid transportation systems that Canadians in those cities would use, we could effectively reduce the energy consumption of the automobile by 25 per cent. Translated to the national scene that would mean a saving of at least 12 per cent to 14 per cent of our oil needs. If that is then projected ten to 15 years hence, we are talking about a dramatic reduction in our reliance on offshore oil.
Lastly we need mass rapid transit systems in our cities because of the quality of life Canadians expect to find in large urban centres. Surely every member in this House has been in an automobile in a traffic jam at rush hour. These traffic jams could be avoided by rapid transit systems. Yet, we are debating a bill that would recapitalize the CNR and there is not a murmur from this government and the minister relating to mass transit systems. It is difficult to understand that a government that has been in power for 15 years in this country has yet to put in place that kind of a national urban transit strategy.
I see the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs in the House. He is from Toronto and I hope he stays around for awhile because I will have some things to say about him.
Just a couple of weeks ago the Premier of Ontario, the Hon. William Davis, took up a chisel officially to start a $58-million program in alterations in Toronto's union station. I do not

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
know whether my friend, the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs was there, but I would not expect so because he would be somewhat embarrassed by the fact that the province of Ontario has had to go it alone. I do not live in Toronto but I have been there and I have been to Union Station. Union Station ought to be perserved for history. Sir, that is a usable archive. If hon. members have ever been to Union Station during lunch hour, they will have noticed that it is jammed packed with people. The vision of the Ontario government was its GO Transit service. It has gone it alone to modernize and upgrade the facilities, especially at Union Station.
This government promised $100 million of the $258 million for mass transit systems in this country, and in particular for metro Toronto. Of the $58 million the province is spending, at least $26.5 million should be coming from the federal government as said by those election promises made in June, 1974. We have facts with relation to Toronto. However, there is another city that found it necessary to go it alone, Edmonton. That is as a result of this government reneging on its grandiose statements and promises which it makes so fluently during an election campaign.
The city of Edmonton had to go it alone for $65.9 million. The provincial commitment was $45 million, and $20.9 million for the city of Edmonton. The federal government did not put up even one devalued dollar, in fact not a penny. The province of Alberta and the city of Edmonton pleaded with them to put into place a mass rapid transit system there.
I could speak of the south-west transit study in my city of Winnipeg. That study was undertaken as a direct result of the election promise in 1974. I know the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs is anxious to hear about that. I am sure he is one of the Liberals who hopes these promises will be long forgotten by Canadians.
Because of the promises made during the election campaign in 1974, Manitoba, and in particular Winnipeg, undertook the south-west transit system study to see whether it would be feasible to use existing rail lines owned by CNR and CPR which run from downtown Winnipeg to the university. That is the most heavily populated area of Winnipeg. Phase two, and a million and a half dollars later, the then mayor of Winnipeg, Mayor Juba, a fine man who has done our city proud, received word that the game was off, he would have to go it alone.
What was the result? Neither Winnipeg nor Manitoba has the kinds of funds that it can commit up to $100 million for a mass rapid transit system. The dream of Mayor Juba and of many Winnipeggers of a uni-rail or a rapid transit system went down the drain. A million and a half dollars later, that study had to be shelved because of this government reneging on its promises.
I am going to quote from a document dated June 17, 1974. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has just entered the Chamber. His eyes lit up because he recognized that date. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was speaking in the great city

of Toronto. What I have in my hand is a copy of the very paper that the Prime Minister held in his hand on June 17, 1974, in Toronto. Your Honour will recall that the election was on July 8. We were only a couple of weeks from polling day. I will read only the main points of what the Prime Minister said. I quote:
The Liberal government will-
Notice the word "will", not maybe, hopefully, or "we promise." He did not say the Government of Canada, the government of the nation, but the Liberal government. That did not commit the opposition or the hoped-for Stanfield government. He said:
The Liberal government will pay 100 per cent of the cost of new commuter vehicles manufactured in Canada,.. .
The Liberal government will pay 25 per cent of the capital cost of all vehicles purchased each year for public transit within Canadian cities and which are manufactured in Canada.
Financial support will be made available to encourage Canadian design ...
For Canada's smaller municipalities, the Liberal government will offer assistance ...
Canadian industry will be encouraged to develop "off the shelf' standardized systems ...
The Liberal government will encourage urban transit systems innovations,...
The Liberal government is committed-
I looked up the word "committed" because I wanted to know exactly what the Prime Minister was getting at. I looked it up in both the Oxford and Webster dictionaries. I certainly did not want to be biased in any definition I might find. Forgive me, Mr. Speaker, but I have a cold. Otherwise I would be much more adamant in what lam saying today.

speechtext: More eloquent, too.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
The Solicitor General (Mr. Blais) has just entered the chamber. He speaks well in both official languages, but says nothing in either. I am glad he has come into the chamber to be refreshed with regard to these Liberal government pledges and promises of June 17, 1974. I was talking about the word "committed". It means entrust. The Prime Minister was saying that if the Canadian people would elect a Liberal government, that government would entrust. That is a very interesting word for this government.
The Liberal government is committed to removing the 12 per cent sales tax-
That was four years ago.
The Liberal government will offer the best use of existing railway rights of way and track in urban and suburban areas for new commuter and urban transit lines-
It was that which precipitated the south-west transit study in Winnipeg. On February 16, in Toronto, that was scrapped after a cost of $1.5 million. What is a million and a half dollars to this government which this year is spending $10 billion it does not have?
The Liberal government will rapidly implement the Railway Relocation Act, to ensure that railway relocation in cities also contributes to the right kinds of city growth.
I am not saying the only reason the people in Toronto voted Liberal was because of that statement of the Prime Minister,
May 10, 1978

but it certainly gave them something to hope for, a vision, a dream, a quality of life, that they would no longer have to ride in automobiles along crowded streets during rush hour.
It was promised that the Union Station would be upgraded. There would no longer be the mass confusion that exists in Union Station. In large part the hopes of Torontonians were placed in this government because of those promises made on June 17, 1974. This government was re-elected. I do not know exactly how many members it has from metro-Toronto, but I expect the number would be around 18 or 19. Two years passed. Then came the black day for Toronto, indeed for all urban centres in this country which had placed hope and trust in this government as far as urban transportation is concerned.
On February 16, 1977, at eleven o'clock in the morning, the then minister of finance, Mr. Macdonald, made an announcement. The headline in the Globe and Mail for that date read "Promised in 1974, $290 Million Transit Plan Dead". It was finished. Two years before that the cities and municipalities were told that the government had a scheme, that they could count on the government. Two years later, when half the cities across this country had proceeded with plans, they were told that the government was withdrawing, the game was over. First they were in, then were out; now they don't know. This is the kind of government we have.
Here it is May 10, 1978, and we have not heard a peep, not even a squeak, about urban transportation. I expect the game plan is to wait until the writ is issued. Then they will take this sheet I have been reading from, resurrect these policies, and reprint it word for word. Well, it will not work. Canadians will not buy it. They do not trust the government.
I have other articles here. This is from the Globe and Mail of March 3, 1977: "The Liberals Might Break Ranks Over Transit Grants". The subheading reads: "Broken Election Promise Upsets two MPs." There was a great stir among the backbenchers of the Liberal party at that time. The members from Toronto were not going to stand for what was happening. They were elected on this promise and they were determined to stand up and be counted. There was a revolution, and one of the leaders was the hon. member for York East (Mr. Col-lenette). We understood that all the Toronto members were joining. The ranks of the dissidents were growing daily to swell the strength of the revolution and oblige the government to make good the promise it gave in 1974. Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say that the revolution was stamped out. It failed.
I want to go over the list of those revolutionaries and name them by their constituencies. There was the Minister of State for Small Business, the hon. member for Mississauga (Mr. Abbott). He failed. There was the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni). The hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia) failed. The hon. member for York East failed. The revolution he started was stamped out. The Minister of National Defence, the hon. member for York North (Mr. Danson) failed. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) failed. The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Railway Act
Kaplan) failed. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Martin) failed. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services, the hon. member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) failed. The hon. member for Scarborough-East (Mr. O'Connell) failed. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Philbrook) failed. I remember him.
I raised this very matter only a couple of days after this bitter blow to the urban centres of this country and I remember the hon. member for Halton getting to his feet to speak- he, certainly, did not intend to allow this promise made in June, 1974 to be forgotten. He failed as well.
The Secretary of State from St. Paul's (Mr. Roberts) failed. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, from Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) failed. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Sharp) failed. The hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery) failed. I want to get all this on the record because those are the ridings which returned members of parliament who supported the Liberal government which on June 17, 1974, promised through its leader to provide a mass rapid transit system to meet the needs of the urban centres of Canada, in particular, Toronto. Yet today we are asked to debate a bill which has to do with the recapitalization of the CNR involving the transfer of millions of dollars from debt to equity. The government expects the opposition to agree to this notwithstanding the fact that the promise made in the election campaign of 1974 has been so flagrantly broken.
Bearing in mind the dearth of information which has been given to parliament on this subject, I think it is an act of responsibility on the part of my hon. friend from Lisgar to move that the bill be given a six-month hoist. It is idle for the government to expect us to pass this bill in the absence of proper information on the subject. Moreover, as my hon. friend has stated, the CNR will probably make a profit this year in any event. I oppose the measure for these reasons, but mainly because I, for one, along with most of the people who live in this country, cannot trust the government to do what it pledges it will do for the people.

The bill should have a six-month hoist and the government should have a 20-year hoist. My hon. friend from Selkirk said the government had made some commitment in 1974 in Toronto. That had a certain right sound to it.

He said he was only prepared to assist Newfoundland in improving and renovating the trans-Canada highway to the extent of 50 per cent of the cost. He brutalized the Newfoundland government into finally surrendering and accepting his offer-it was 50 per cent or nothing, and our government certainly cannot afford to spend $250 million on the trans-Canada highway in the next ten years out of its own coffers. So they had to accept this 50 per cent offer. The new slogan in Newfoundland is, "We'll drive at risk and with a bang until we're rid of Otto Lang." That time is coming. If the Prime Minister does his duty as a patriot and as a citizen of Canada he will call an election tomorrow and we shall terminate this whole business. Members opposite who want a copy of my remarks concerning the trans-Canada highway can just notify my office and we will send a copy to any member who missed my speech on that occasion.

To come back to transportation, Mr. Speaker, and this bill which deals with the CNR which is in all facets of transportation-and therefore we can be in all facets of transportation in discussing this-there was a commission appointed in March of 1977 to consider the state of transportation facilities in Newfoundland, the Sullivan commission, chaired by Dr. Art Sullivan, and an interim report is to be made by that commission by the end of May to the minister. He has been a railway union leader for many years and has done a lot of work for the federal government on commissions and groups like that studying transportation questions. Esau has become seriously ill. The commission is putting in an interim report based on the recommendations that he had agreed to up to the time he became ill. They are naturally hoping that he will be back with them to complete the report, but the final report will not be in for some six or eight months because of it. Now, when the commission was appointed it was hoped that it would conclude its report by the end of '77. That has not been possible, so in speaking today, Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to express my hope that Mr. Thoms' health will improve and to let him know that we are thinking of him and that many people in Newfoundland are thinking of him and hoping that he is going to recover and continue his valuable contribution to our province.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there was a royal commission on transportation in Newfoundland in 1962, and it must have been a royal commission that had never heard of the phrase "user pay" that became the motto of the present Minister of Transport.
