It became the motto of Otto. It's going to become the political death of Otto also.
There was an article in the Newfoundland Telegram on March 5, 1977. There is a cartoon in it about government taking over rail service, and somebody's got marked here, "It's too bad Newfoundland is not a part of Canada". Mr. Speaker, I come from the only province of Canada that has no railway passenger service. It was assassinated by the Liberal government in 1967 with the connivance of the then Liberal premier, Mr. Smallwood. He was an accessory before the fact and an accessory after the fact to the killing and the assassination of the railway passenger service in Newfoundland, and therefore he bears a lot of guilt particularly, Mr. Speaker, because in return he got an inferior trans-Canada highway that is less
May 10, 1978

than the quality of the highway in every other province of Canada and which now in 1978 is a fearsome sight indeed as you drive along that highway because of what has happened with the traffic it has had to bear in the last ten years.
This commission was the MacPherson commission of 1962 appointed by the right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert and his government. They did their study about ten years after we entered confederation, and they said, and I quote:
The situation in Newfoundland is a special case distinct from the rest of Canada.
That was a finding of this commission, and our case is distinct from the rest of Canada. They went on to say, and I quote again:
The situation in Newfoundland is such that it may prove necessary in the short run to eliminate competition, to favour by subsidization or special treatment one mode (of transport) against another... and to do other things that would be totally unacceptable in other parts of Canada ...
The Liberal government certainly adopted part of that quotation because they have done things that would be totally unacceptable in other parts of Canada. They did away with our rail passenger service, Mr. Speaker. That is one of the things they did, so they did not carry out that recommendation, but they decided to do things that would not be acceptable in any other part of Canada, and we are not taking it lying down, Mr. Speaker. Another thing that they did and the minister did-and this minister is responsible-this Minister of Transport was the minister on July 16, 1976, when an order in council was passed here at Ottawa removing the CN bus service which had replaced the railway passenger service, removing the CN bus passenger service from the jurisdiction of the Newfoundland Public Utilities Commission which had regulated their affairs and services and putting them under the Canadian Transport Commission.
The Canadian Transport Commission, the federal body, since July of 1976 has been in charge of rates and jurisdiction over the CN bus service. Mr. Speaker, that was done without consultation with the Newfoundland government. It was an abysmal example of barbaric federalism, of Kung-Fu federalism. It was a barbaric act of arrogance here at Ottawa just to do that without consultation with the province. And what has been the result? The CN bus service has been removed from the Public Utilities Commission of Newfoundland, and it has been left by the Canadian Transport Commission to do what it wishes. The first thing that happened, Mr. Speaker, was that they got an 8 per cent increase immediately, and then, Mr. Speaker, last year the CN bus-yes, 1977-the CN bus system decided that they had to have another increase of 15 per cent in bus fares down in Newfoundland. So they had gotten 8 per cent in March of 1977. All right, Mr. Speaker, that is an 8 per cent increase in March, 1977, for the CN bus system. Then they applied in August to the Canadian Transport Commission for another 15 per cent hike in their rates in what they charged consumers in Newfoundland, and they wanted that on October 1.
Mr. Speaker, do you know that the commission came to Newfoundland to have a hearing, I believe, in November of
Railway Act
1977? October or November. The commission said that they had to give them the 15 per cent increase, that they didn't have the power to stop them, although they hadn't concluded their hearing. They hadn't made a decision. The commission said that they were going to allow the CN bus system to have another 15 per cent increase in fares, and they would give their decision later. I believe the last hearing was in March. Sorry, the last hearing was held down in Newfoundland in late November, 1977. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is December, January, February, March, April-this is May. It's about six months. December, January, February, March, April-yes, five months, almost six months since they held their hearings and, Mr. Speaker, I checked again today with the Canadian Transport Commission, and there is no decision yet on that application, and the CN for the last five months has imposed these higher fares, the 15 per cent hike, and the Canadian Transport Commission has not brought down a decision. Well, what are we in Newfoundland? Are we to be treated as nothings by the Minister of Transport opposite and his federal agencies here in Ottawa?

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: They just don't care.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
All the CN has to do to get a fare increase is to make the application, and the Canadian Transport Commission says they can do nothing about it, and this commission comes and holds hearings and does not give an answer and does not make a judgment or a decision for five months. I say, Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Transport and the Canadian Transport Commission .cannot do better than that, he should put CN bus services back under the jurisdiction of the Public Utilities Commission of Newfoundland where they were not allowed to have increase until the rate hearings were over and the board had made a decision. Since the Minister of Transport took them away from the jurisdiction of Newfoundland in July of 1976 they have had increases in fares of 23 per cent, Mr. Speaker-23 per cent-and they are getting away with murder. They can do what they like.
Either there is something wrong with the Canadian Transport Commission, either they have not got enough personnel, they have too much work, or the committee that deals with these things has got too many hearings. Surely this is not right that the CN can apply and get an increase in their bus fares last October and the committee has the hearings in the fall of 1977 and there is still no announced decision. What is to happen if they decide they should not have had 15 per cent? How are you going to be able to prove who were the bus passengers and decide how much each bus passenger should get back if the board finds they should not have taken that 15 per cent increase?
Now, Mr. Speaker, that is just one example of how we are being treated in Newfoundland by the Canadian Department of Transport and its minister and the Canadian government. We do not like it, and we are not putting up with it. We have heard no one from the other side say anything about it. It is left to us poor people over here in opposition to raise our voices against this high-handed and arbitrary treatment by the

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
Canadian Transport Commission and the CN bus service. They are not strange bedfellows, but they are certainly in bed together if better than this cannot be done.
So I bring that to the attention of the House, Mr. Speaker, as some of the things that have been done in Newfoundland. It is totally unacceptable in other parts of Canada, but because it is down in Newfoundland, it is out of sight, out of mind. Only when we, members here, are aggravated or provoked, does anybody up here hear about it, and even then it is difficult to get coverage on the mainland, unless it is under Standing Order 43.
The MacPherson commission of 1962 went on to say the following. It pointed out that no part in Canada had prospered until it had good transportation facilities. It stated:
The history of Canada is replete with examples of massive public spending on transport facilities such as canals, railways and more recently highways and airports... There is no question that the economy of Newfoundland cannot develop at a satisfactory pace without more transportation facilities. A highway network of the size necessary is beyond the present (1962) resources of Newfoundland ... The situation calls for assistance by the federal government and there are enough precedents for such a program.
This is still the situation 16 years later. The MacPherson commission's principles were never implemented. The Minister of Transport is not interested in doing anything in Newfoundland except to decrease his expenditures and costs. He is trying to crush with an iron heel the minister of transport in Newfoundland, and he is threatening the Newfoundland government that if they do not accept 50 per cent for reconstructing the trans-Canada highway, they will get nothing, not a sou. He sweetened it by saying that they would help Newfoundland with the cash flow, if it surrendered, which Newfoundland had to do, that the province would get 75 per cent of the money spent, the following year, a different percentage, and the third year 50 per cent, or in the third year it would decline to 25 per cent. In other words, the Newfoundland government will get 75 per cent now, but over a three year period it will receive a contribution of 50 per cent from the Government of Canada.
The provincial minister of transport has accepted this on the condition that if the Sullivan commission makes a contrary recommendation or recommends that the federal government should give more assistance, the Minister of Transport will agree that the trans-Canada highway can be opened up. Of course, the Minister of Transport wil not be here when the final report comes in. God willing, and the public of Canada willing, we will be over there dealing with that matter fairly and justly next fall.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Some people think that Newfoundland should lose its rail service altogether. We are not losing the rail service. I do not care what any royal commission recommends, there will be a rail service in Newfoundland and it will not be taken away from us. Unless the rail service is totally abandoned in Canada, it will not be abandoned in Newfoundland.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
We know what CN points out. CN did not come out before the commission and say we should abandon the rail service. It stated that their total loss on rail express in 1976 amounted to $24 million. Of that amount, CN rail lost $14 million-$7 million was lost on CN express and $2 million on the road cruiser service, the bus service. The total loss was $24 million. I do not blame the CN entirely for what has happened in these areas; I blame the government for it.
I should like to quote now from the Evening Telegram of Wednesday, September 21, 1977, reporting on CN's presentation to the commission. It says:
CN, like many other witnesses before the commission, feels the only possible way the rail service can be improved is by direct federal subsidy for losses.
We know that the minister does not like to hear that. This is a rail service that will not break even, not without a lot of money spent on it first. Mr. Gratwick of the CN told the commission that in Newfoundland we should do the same as is done out west. This sounds like an excellent suggestion, but I do not know that it is as easy as this. He said:
You apply to abandon a railway and then you get a federal subsidy... That's what happens.
If that is what happens out west, we want some of the action. We have no objection whatsoever to CN applying, or we can apply, to abandon the railway and that the federal government should then come in and give us a federal subsidy so that the railway can operate the same as it does out west.
The article goes on to read:
He suggested the same argument might not stand up in Newfoundland, but added, "I think it's worth a try."
The CN Railway in Newfoundland was owned by the Newfoundland government before 1949. It was taken over by the Canadian government and is operated by CN. The Canadian government should meet the deficits if deficits are unavoidable, but the Canadian government has not done that. The Canadian government has allowed losses on the Newfoundland railway to be absorded by CN, and CN, in their attempt to lessen their losses, has done everything it can to trash the Newfoundland railway, to let it go down and to put the freight and the cargo on the highway. It does not want more losses. So it is up to the Government of Canada to meet these losses directly.
The article goes on to read:
He said an application can be made for the abandonment of a "branch line".
In Newfoundland, of course, the railway might not be considered a branch line. However, if the government wants to consider it a branch line, it can. That will have to be the solution in Newfoundland.
The railway's share of the freight traffic in Newfoundland declined from 87 per cent in 1971 to 61 per cent in 1976, and it has declined more since then. The number of employees on the railway in Newfoundland has declined considerably, by at least 200, according to the evidence before the Sullivan commission, that is, on the railway part of the operation alone, not including all CN services. In 1974 there were 1,891 employees with CN Rail; in 1976 there were 1,715, that is, 176 less. We
May 10, 1978

do not want this attrition to continue. Once the Sullivan commission has reported, we want the government to confirm that the railway service is continuing. Improvements will be made.
The railway is necessary because heavy freight and cargo should be moved by rail. Also, the railway is found to be a better conserver of energy than having everything hauled by truck or car. There is railway service in every other province of Canada-we want it in Newfoundland. That is what we want the government to say and do if the commission's report comes out before we take over.
A loan of $100 million was made by the government to CNR in 1952 with no interest charge until 1974 after the government was re-elected. Now there is an interest charge of $5.5 million a year on that loan charged to the Newfoundland service of the railway. When we consider what CN is allegedly losing in Newfoundland, let us remember that the Liberal government imposed a further $5.5 million interest burden on the Newfoundland service in 1974. That has been included in those figures.
What else is the minister doing? He is planning to have the Newfoundland railway abandoned. That is what he hopes will result from the Sullivan commission report. He has allowed CN to do everything they want in removing CN employees of CN Marine and other services, moving them to Moncton and other places, moving them out of Newfoundland. 1 do not know whether the minister has been successful in this as yet, but he wants to remove federal participation in ferry services in Newfoundland. That is spelled ferry, not fairy, the leprechaun.
There was an interesting article in the Globe and Mail of May 12, 1977, which pointed out the various subsidies which were paid to waterborne services in Newfoundland and other areas, but principally in Newfoundland. It stated:
The shortfall of the CN operated Newfoundland coastal service alone was $23.9 million.
I do not know whether the article was supposed to lead everyone to conclude that the coastal service in Newfoundland should be eliminated. We know the coastal service cannot break even, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think even the government wants to eliminate it. It pointed out that the ferry service to Port aux Basques required $44.3 million, while the run to Argentia consumed $4.59 million. "Consumed", Mr. Speaker! You see the weasel wording that is supposed to induce the reader to say to himself, "By God, Newfoundlanders are consuming our money at a rapid rate". The run to Argentia consumed $4.59 million. What is the run from Montreal to Toronto consuming? What is the run from Ottawa to Quebec City, if there is one, consuming? What is the run from Montreal to Halifax consuming? We only hear such weasel words when they are talking about service to Newfoundland.
Is that an argument to do away with the service from the mainland to Newfoundland, to Argentia and Port aux
Railway Act
Basques, because it loses money? We know it loses money. The ferry to Prince Edward Island loses money also.
Then they go on to say that the privately operated service from St. Barbe, Newfoundland, to Blanc Sablon Bay received $219,000 last year. The federal government now wants Newfoundland to take that over, Mr. Speaker. It wants to impose and push this burden on the province of Canada which can least afford any additional financial burdens imposed on it. The honourable crowd opposite who do not mind their own deficits in billions, are trying to push a $219,000 deficit, if you go on the vessel ferry from St. Barbe in northern Newfoundland to Blanc Sablon, on to the province. Then they say the ferry from Burnside and St. Brendan's-these are islands-St. Brendan's is an island off the coast of Newfoundland-they want to push $82,000 on to Newfoundland; and Cobbs Arm and Change Islands, $86,000. They want to push that on to Newfoundland. These are all in the district of the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Baker).
Then the minister wants to push on to Newfoundland the cost of the service between Carmanville and Fogo Island, $173,000; and from Greenspond to Badger's Quay, $55,750; and from Portugal Cove to Bell Island, $993,000; and from Middle Bay Islands to St. Patrick's, $209,000. All of these ferry services, Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport opposite now wants the Newfoundland government to pick up, assume, and carry that financial burden. What is wrong with the man? Has he any sense of honour or any sense of observing any commitments that this government has got?
Of the several millions of dollars of subsidies that the federal government has been paying out for many years, many of them were instituted because, Mr. Speaker, certain communities were resettled and the coastal boat service no longer went to these other communities. In other words, these services were instituted to assist the federal government which was saving money because the coastal service did not have to go to a lot of other small communities that were being resettled. Now ten years later the Minister of Transport of Canada said to the Newfoundland government, "You have got to take over these ferry services, and you have got to meet their losses". I mean, the man is a Barbarossa. He is a relic from the dark ages. He is Hagar the Hun gone berserk. This is user-pay to the utmost, Mr. Speaker. The Canadian public would have to be flagellating itself to re-elect the likes of them and put them back in power in Ottawa, Mr. Speaker. It would certainly be flagellating Newfoundland and giving us a whipping. The whip will be back on our backs if they are ever returned to office again. Now, Mr. Speaker, those are the certain ferry services the minister wants to force back on Newfoundland.
Then there is another peculiar group of subsidies, $3.6 million paid by the Government of Canada toward the major steamship service between Montreal, St. John's, and Corner Brook. There is a subsidy paid to Clarke Transportation. It has been going on for years. It is for them to provide a service from Montreal to St. John's and Corner Brook. The initial subsidy was $7 a ton. It was intended as interim assistance to Clarke Transportation. That subsidy has now gone to $15.64 a ton for

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
every ton of cargo they move between Montreal, St. John's and Corner Brook during the shipping season. That increase is not enough. Apparently Clarke wants the subsidy increased. They have a 13-year subsidy contract with the government now. It expires in 1986,1 am advised. They want the subsidy increased from $15.64 a ton up to $25 a ton, I think it is.
At the old rate of $15.64 it cost the federal government $3.5 million two years ago for that subsidy. Now Clarke wants a much bigger subsidy, because they want to get another ship to put on the Montreal-St. John's run. They want a bigger subsidy and a longer commitment because of that.
I took this matter up with the minister. I am advised that the government does not control the rates charged by Clarke. They are only indirectly controlled. Clarke files its rates, and the Liberal subsidy can be changed, depending on the revenues and profits of the company. The government has access to Clarke's books in the annual subsidy review. This is all done behind the scenes. We have no access to know what they are making or what they are not making.
In the meantime, other shipping lines have started services from the mainland to Newfoundland by sea: Newfoundland Container Lines, Ltd., owned by A. Harvey & Company, from Halifax to St. John's; and Chimo Container Service, owned by Chimo Shipping, Ltd. has inaugurated a service from Montreal to St. John's, using the vessel Sir John Crosbie.
Let me say that Chimo Shipping Ltd. is owned by relatives of mine. I have no interest in it. I mention that because when I took this matter up with the minister in June, 1977, as is some people's wont, the first thing I saw was a story in the St. John's Evening Telegram. It was a statement by the manager of Newfoundland Steamships, the Clarke company in St. John's, one Elmer Edison, indicating that I have ulterior motives. He said that I never spoke before the Crosbies started their own service. Now, Mr. Speaker, I am an independent operator. 1 never spoke before because I was not a federal member before. Well, I am a federal member now, and I do not care if Chimo Shipping is owned by the Crosbies, the Smiths, the Langs, the Chretiens, or who owns it. If I think this is not in the public interest, I am going to bring it forward in this House.
No pip-squeak of a Clarke's manager in St. John's is going to frighten me by suggesting that I have some ulterior motive. I say this House is entitled to know what is happening with this subsidy to Clarke. The Chimo Shipping service is operating without a subsidy. The Harvey service is operating without a subsidy. Clarke is getting a subsidy which we know cost $3.6 million in 1976. Are we going to know how the rates are regulated? If there is going to be a continued subsidy of rates why are other companies not entitled to a subsidy? What value is the consumer getting through these rates?
Is Clarke going to get another contract for higher subsidy rates? How are we going to ensure that the consumer gets the benefit, and it is not just a benefit to Clarke? That is what we want to know. How are we going to be assured that it is going to reduce the cost of cargo moving into Newfoundland and moving out? I do not know what has happened with their application to get an increase in subsidies, or what will happen

with those services. It is time that there was some information given to this House and to the transport committee of it.
There is another matter I want to mention. I do not want to take too long here because this is our last day, I believe.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

speechtext: Your last stand.

speechtext: Order!

speechtext:
One never knows with the electorate. They are very fickle, but I hope to be back, Mr. Speaker.
I happened to receive a letter. I am sure most members did. It was dated April 25, and it was from the Canadian Railways Employees' Pension Association. It brought up questions to do with their pension funds and whether the unfunded liability is going to be met in full. They seem to be quite concerned about it. Before concluding, I just want to point out that I brought that matter up before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, when we had the superintendent of insurance of the Department of Finance before us. I asked the superintendent if they also supervised pension funds, whether he was familiar with the CN pension fund, and whether he was satisfied with it. I am looking for the relevant page. At page 27:12 I asked Mr. Humphrys if he had any reason to be concerned about the soundness of the CN plan. He said:
No, Mr. Chairman, wc believe the plan is being managed and financed in accordance with the requirements of the Pension Benefits Standards Act and we believe adequate provision is being made to cover the liabilities.
Then I asked him, if I sent him a copy of the brief, would he look at it and give me his comments on it. He said that he would.
On May 5 I did write Mr. Humphrys and asked him to examine this submission from the Employees' Pension Association. I asked him to advise me whether, in his opinion, it is being managed and financed properly, and whether adequate provision had been made to cover liabilities; he had said that in committee. I have asked him to deal with the points and fears expressed in this brief from the railway pensioners. Certainly as members of this House we have to concern ourselves and make sure their concerns are needless, we hope, and therefore I have asked Mr. Humphrys to do that and he has said he would. He has already given the opinion that he does not think there is anything to be concerned about and that the liabilities to pensioners can be met.
I want the people who live in St. John's West who are railway pensioners to know that I share their concern, and I
May 10, 1978

am going to pursue this matter for them as they would expect me to do. I am sure other members take the same position in respect of pensioners of the CN with whom they are dealing.
I am going to come to a close because there are other speakers, and I think we want to conclude this today. I won't go into all the other points I could make on transportation in Newfoundland. We are concerned about a replacement for the William Carson which sank a year ago. It was very important to the ferry service of Newfoundland and she has not been replaced as yet.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Like the Frank Moore; that should be replaced.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am talking about the William Carson, not the Broadbent, she has already floundered. I say replace the Carson with the Broadbent. That would be a good idea. He is going to need his bottom scraped before the election is over, Mr. Speaker. There has been no vessel ordered that we know of; the construction of no vessel has been ordered to replace the William Carson. There should be a vessel ordered from a Canadian shipyard, and it should be ordered now because of the time lag, and a vessel should be chartered in the meantime.
We are not satisfied with the ferry service to Argentia, nor are we satisfied with the ferry service generally from the mainland to Newfoundland. There are many complaints and I cannot go into them today, but it is not a satisfactory service for the travelling public. It has very badly affected the tourist trade. Tourists do not like to go through what they have to go through to get to Newfoundland and from it with their cars, when the tourist season comes. Because there are other speakers I will not go into anything else except to say this, Mr. Speaker. This is my last speech in the House, I feel sure-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext: Perhaps I could finish. This is my last speech in this House on this side. At the next session of the House I hope to speak from the benches opposite. It is my wish and hope that this House will be dissolved tomorrow and we can get on to the business of saving Canada from the hon. gentlemen opposite.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO AMEND AND REPEAL CERTAIN STATUTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate on third reading of Bill C-17 concerning the amortization of $808 million in CN debt. I support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Murta), that this bill be given a six-month hoist.
When speaking on second reading of Bill C-17 I expressed a number of the problems that concern people of the constituency of Churchill about the track running from The Pas to Churchill, some 509 miles, and from The Pas to Lynn Lake, another 170 miles. I am only going to deal with that one small segment of the mass problem of the CN. Of course it has the same problem just mentioned by the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie). This problem runs all the way from Cobbs Arm Island in Newfoundland to Pukatawagan in
Railway Act
northern Manitoba; the same problem seems to exist everywhere.
The CN's obligation, as far as I am concerned, is to provide service to all areas of Canada. What we have seen over the past five years is service which has now reached the point of desperation in many parts of the Churchill constituency. In that constituency between The Pas and Churchill, the 509 miles of railway, we have observed communities such as Thicket Portage, Pikwitonei, Ilford, Gillam and Churchill without highway access, but with a service provided by the CNR faced with no competitive rates. As a result it has been ripping off the people of these communities. I want to get into that particular aspect a little later in my remarks.
We have just noticed very recently, now that passenger service has been turned over to VIA Rail, that excursion trains going to Churchill this summer will continue to have the same rates that applied last year. This is great for the people who are going to be travelling to Churchill on those excursion trains. We certainly welcome those tourists who come up to see that great sea port of Churchill which is now being underutilized because this government cannot seem to get its act in order, using that port to full capacity in respect of grain shipments.
While these excursion rates are to remain unchanged from last year, the Car-Go-Rail rates which have been in effect for some time will be discontinued. When we talk of Car-Go-Rail rates we refer to the main concern of the CNR being with the Toronto to Winnipeg run. That seems to be its major market area. What does this really mean to communities such as Gillam, Ilford, Pukatawagan, Pikwitonei and Thicket Portage where there is no off-rail transportation whatsoever? These communities must use the rail to transport their vehicles out to a highway system.
On April 29 the CN advised, and I have a copy of that letter, that the Car-Go-Rail rates and services which had been provided by the passenger division for the past number of years would be discontinued. Insofar as the major market areas such as Toronto to Winnipeg served by Car-Go-Rail in the past are concerned, CN will be announcing a new service called "transAuto". I do not know if this has anything to do with the minister because it is spelled "A-u-t-o", but that is probably the only way the minister could get his name into it. The letter suggests that transAuto will be substantially different from Car-Go-Rail in that it will be available as a whole sale service only to household moving companies, car rental companies, and similar organizations. Apparently private individuals wishing to move their vehicles between the points covered will have to go to one of these companies for retail service.
The letter goes on to state that CN recognizes it must continue to provide a retail service to residents of points in northern Manitoba not served by roads, and to meet this need it is publishing new freight rates to cover the movement of private passenger vehicles effective May 1, and I have a copy of this. Between Thompson and Gillam the rate is to be $87 per unit one way, and between Thompson and Churchill it is to
5298

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
be $128 per unit one way. Under the Car-Go-Rail system an individual taking his car out of Churchill or Gillam, and those are the two places referred to here, could buy a ticket, put his car on the train, ride with his car and have his car unloaded, and continue on his way. This really provided a much needed service to those communities that do not have access to highway transportation.
This letter goes on to state:
'
If a need develops for rates to and from other points not served by highway, they will be provided as required.
I would say that, instead of waiting for the rates to be provided as required, there are still the rates that must be worked out between Ilford and Thompson, Pikwitonei and Thompson, Thicket Portage and Thompson as well as from Pukatawagan to The Pas and Sherridon to The Pas. These people are also in the same situation. They cannot get their vehicles out unless they put them on the railway.
The letter ends up by saying:
Our personnel are being notified immediately of the availability of these rates after 1 May, and we will advise the media in the hope that they will inform the general public.
Well, Mr. Speaker, many of the communities in northern Manitoba do not have daily newspapers. They now have radio stations and television, but an announcement like this would probably not be carried over the particular television program that might be aired in northern Manitoba.
The letter from the CNR was dated April 12. On April 25 a letter was sent to the vice-president of the prairie region. This letter was from Mr. Banman, the minister of transportation in Manitoba. Mr. Banman in his letter pointed out his concern over the withdrawal of Car-Go-Rail service as a result of the transfer of rail passenger service to VIA Rail. Mr. Banman said in part:
I appreciate the fact that CN has introduced alternative arrangements to provide for the essential movement of vehicles between points in northern Manitoba not served by roads. However, we do have several concerns on this issue.
These are the same concerns that I raised in this House under Standing Order 43 as reported at page 5048 of Hansard.
Mr. Banman went on to say:
I note that the charge per vehicle effective May 1 has been set at $87 between Thompson and Gillam, and $128 between Thompson and Churchill. This represents increases of $27 and $59 per vehicle respectively over the charges currently applicable under the Car-Go-Rail plan. These increases appear to be rather excessive. Also, the absence of specific commodity rates to cover shipments between other points could result in the application of extremely high charges under class or express rate structures. There is also a requirement for maintaining rates between some northern communities served by road as a result of circuitous routes as well as long distances through desolate and isolated terrain.
In view of the foregoing, I would respectfully ask that Items 11650 and 11880 of tariff CNR W.l 150 be reinstated as soon as possible. In addition, as it will be some time before VIA absorbs local passenger services, I would also ask for your consideration in extending the Car-Go-Rail plan at least until such time the transfer is made.
What has happened here is that the CN in their expertise and before VIA Rail had actually taken over was going to implement these particular changes using the transAuto rates and the new rates set up by VIA Rail thereby doing away with the Car-Go-Rail system.
On May 3 Mr. Banman received a letter from the CNR prairie region manager, a copy of which I have here. It says:
I would like to acknowledge receipt of your letter of 25 April, concerning the withdrawal of Gar-Go-Rail services.
Due to some problems experienced in the establishment of our proposed transAuto service, Car-Go-Rail service on our main line routes has been extended to 31 May.
Because of my intervention and the intervention of the minister of transport from Manitoba, the CN is now saying that the rates will not be in effect on May 1, but will be extended to May 31.
He goes on to say:
It is anticipated that on 1 June VIA will assume full responsibility for rail passenger operations including those to northern Manitoba.
I would like to point out here that when people talk about a re-amortization of the CNR's $8.8 million debt, what they are really asking for is that the CN not forget that they have to provide a service. It is their mandate to provide service to areas that have no other means of transportation. I can assure you if there were other means of transportation out of those particular communities I probably would not get a single complaint because, after complaining for years about the poor service the CNR has supplied to those communities, the people have given up in total frustration.
The letter from the CNR goes on:
In response to your request that we extend the Car-Go-Rail plan until such time as the transfer is made, I have arranged for the freight rates on private passenger automobiles between Thompson, Gillam and Churchill to be reduced to the existing Car-Go-Rail level for the month of May, and enclose a copy of CNR Limited Freight Tariff W.4190 which publishes these rates. I should point out that these rates do not require the purchase of a passenger ticket, as was the case under Car-Go-Rail.
Regarding your comments on the rate levels that will take effect on 1 June, I would like to point out that the Car-Go-Rail charges were in effect for many years without increase and were, of course, an integral part of a rail passenger service package. These rates were very substantially below the costs of a freight operation.
I can appreciate that the Car-Go-Rail system was used right across Canada and that the major part of it was between Toronto and Winnipeg, but there are still the northern communities-and I am sure there are some in other provinces- that have no off-highway transportation. The people must use CNR to transport their vehicles when they go out on their annual leave. It is going to be a costly operation when these rates take effect.
As I specified before, the rate from Gillam to Thompson is going up $27, and the rate from Churchill to Thompson is going up $59. That places a real hardship on the people who want to take their families out for a vacation and who want to move their private vehicles. I am sure a lot of people who do travel out of these particular communities would be very happy to sit down with the officials and discuss this particular aspect because it certainly is a burden on them, and they have
[Mr. Smith (Churchill).)
May 10, 1978

no other means of transportation. The CNR is taking advantage of these people, and I would like to see a system set up where the cargo rail rate would still remain in place.
What irritates the people living in these isolated communities is that they must use this particular means of transporting their vehicles out, and yet VIA Rail or CNR says they are going to keep excursion rates for tourists coming into the north the same as last year, but they are going to increase the rate to move a private vehicle when you want to go out on holidays. VIA Rail has given absolutely no consideration to the people living in the north who have to use the facilities. They are the ones who have to bear the burden, but the tourists get the break.
To show the shortsightedness of the CNR, in the same letter in the last paragraph they gave an example to illustrate the number of vehicles that might be moved from any particular community. Of all places the example was Cranberry Portage and the number of vehicles transported from there to Lynn Lake. Everyone living up in that country knows that there is a road from Cranberry Portage to Lynn Lake and there is no need to move a vehicle by railway between those two communities. They say that they cannot justify running a service between Cranberry Portage and Lynn Lake for the simple reason there were only two vehicles moved in the year 1977. That just goes to show that people who live in communities with road access will not use that system. I am looking at the people who must use that system, and who have no other alternative.
Another colleague of mine wants to wrap up this debate. But I would just like to say that we have experienced exactly what the CNR is attempting to do by using the transAuto system to change the rates. We are moving private vehicles out of the north where people have no alternative. That is the same sort of thing the CNR tried to do by eliminating the station agents from those particular communities, Thicket Portage, Pikwitonei, Ilford, Gillam and Sherridon. The CNR arbitrarily made a decision they would move the station agents out of those particular communities. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, the people who live in those isolated communities must depend on the CNR for their freight, mail, express, groceries, and they were heard from. They went to the CNR and demanded that the railway come into those communities just so that the officials who make those decisions could actually see what happens in a small isolated community and how dependent they are on the railway, and how they give them no consideration whatsoever.
The railway cars would arrive with groceries and the railway employees would heave them out of the train. They would not even bother to set them off carefully. There were complaints of eggs and milk being spilled all over the platform. These were items needed by families. Those people in these communities were successful in getting the CNR to withdraw that decision to close those particular stations and remove the station agents. Once the communities made their representations the
Railway Act
CNR saw just how essential those services were to the communities.
This is what I would like to see, and I would challenge those particular communities now. I will certainly give them my support to take the CNR to task and have those rates remain the same as they are now under the Car-Go-Rail system.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I promise that I will finish in good time to have the vote and to have our supper.
I might say that I am happy to speak on this amendment on final reading of Bill C-17. I would like to put on the record some of the fears and thoughts I have as a western Canadian, particularly in regard to the constituency which I represent which is served almost wholly by the Canadian National Railways.
In the last few years in the eastern prairies it would appear that the CNR has acted as if it wanted to abandon most of its railway lines and to give up the job of transporting goods and providing services for the rural communities. First of all we had the Servo centres which were brought in by order of the CTC. This was to phase out the station agents. Gradually these agents were phased out, but when they did that they also phased out the person who was the Canadian National's representative in the community to whom businessmen could turn to get their shipments of goods. These people vanished. In their place they put a Servo centre with a long distance connection to Winnipeg.
Unfortunately, they cannot even man the Servo centres all the time. Customers complain that when they would phone there was no answer. I have found out through railway management that there are so few people around that they cannot always man the telephones in the Servo centres. It happens that business that might belong to the CNR goes elsewhere. It is impossible for shippers to get much satisfaction from the Servo centre by telephone.
The CNR Express have gradually reduced their service. I understand from reading about the situation in Saskatchewan that CN Express have suddenly pulled out from there almost overnight. Shipment of small parcels by railway has all but vanished. This may well be by design, and it is perhaps the result of changing attitudes and changing circumstances. In my opinion, most of us feel that the railways want to reduce their traditional role of carrying heavy bulk cargoes such as grain, or at least to reduce the number of branch lines and to restrict the railways to a few major lines in western Canada running through the country so that grain handling will be carried on by large unit handling elevators located at relatively few points on the prairies. Certainly the dispute carried on now concerning the hours of work whereby the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) wants to declare the country elevator managers covered by the 48-hour week will go a long way to speed up the consolidation of the grain handling system.
The railways may well be expecting too much. Maybe farmers will be driven to use trucks, by changes in the railway system, and if farmers must haul their grain 100 miles or so, it
800 3 8-45 Vi

May 10, 1978
Railway Act
is not all that difficult to haul it considerably farther. Everyone has stated that for the western part of the country the railway is far superior to the highway for the hauling of grain. But in fact there are considerable doubts about this and the mere fact that the steel on steel requires much less energy than the rubber on tarmack is not the only factor in the movement of grain.
My observation is that this bill will hasten the relative reduction of importance of railways in the west with rises in the trucking industry, and particularly for individual farmers who will use their own trucks. Indeed, it has now become evident that individual farms of even a quite small size will have to own their own trucks in order to facilitate the movement of their goods throughout western Canada.
When one observes on the highway the various trucks hauling goods belonging to large chain stores such as Safeways or the Federated Cooperatives or implement companies, indeed it is becoming obvious that the necessity for moving goods in western Canada largely must be met by the companies' own trucks. Franchise trucking firms seem to have difficulty delivering goods as to time and price. It is particularly difficult for small firms, especially retail firms, to have their shipments made efficiently and at a reasonable cost. Indeed, it seems as if many small retail outlets on the prairies will have to pick up their own freight in the larger centres and transport it to their retail stores with their own trucks and vehicles.
The Canadian National Railways in this bill are obviously withdrawing from being a major factor in the transportation system of the west except for some trunk lines. There are a number of reasons for this, some of which are inherent and structural. Trucks can deliver goods cheaply and with a much better time schedule in certain ways.
But there are many other reasons why the CN Railways, at least in my area, are finding their role reduced. Railways are by nature monopolies. To have only the railway to ship is not an unmixed blessing. Trucking lends itself tc individuals, to small units of operation whereby the entrepreneurial spirit can certainly thrive much more than in the rigidity of a large organization such as the CNR. Wage structures are more variable and efficiencies are perhaps easier to come by.
In the matter of management the CNR has obviously one serious fault so far as western Canada is concerned. It is the fact that the management is concentrated in Montreal, and that the concentration in Quebec of management has a serious and detrimental effect on the efficiency of the railways in western Canada. Perhaps it is partly because of geographical, cultural, and linguistic difference. But to have the management so closely controlled in the city of Montreal where railways in the east must compete mostly with water, and when in fact the largest operation of railway activity is concentrated in western Canada, means that management is at a serious disadvantage in dealing with the prairies. Certainly the attitude of the president and management in Montreal, and their actions so far as they affect the west, indicate they have little concept of what is the actual fact there, otherwise they would be doing things differently.

I understand that in years gone by the western region was semi-autonomous and while the final authority rested in Montreal for practical purposes, in the day to day running of the rail line it rested fairly firmly in Winnipeg. There are great disadvantages to the present situation, in that it is much better to manage with on-the-spot knowledge compared to the alternative of a thousand miles away with people who are not familiar with the circumstances in western Canada.
Discussion with many railway employees, and particularly with middle and senior management, although they were reluctant to say much due to their fear of retaliation and jot discrimination, indicates that many railway employees in the west are suspicious and uncertain and, in fact, at times are openly resentful of the policies foisted on them by a management based in Montreal making decisions. There was at one time a considerable body of loyalty, trust, and pride in the work force, but this seems to have gone.
Resentment against management is rife, and indeed many railway workers are looking for means only of finishing out their careers and obtaining other security before moving. Employee morale has probably never been lower. Many of the decisions made affecting the running of the railways make little sense. Sometimes these decisions appear only to be made for the sake of doing something. In any case, railways are greatly cutting themselves off from the communities they serve.
In this legislation, the railway is in fact being forgiven a debt of $800 million. It will make its financial appearance considerably better and it would seem to have a much better chance of overruling its main competition, the Canadian Pacific Railway on one hand and, on the other hand, moving into the trucking field in order to squeeze out independents and the myriad of small trucking concerns across this land.
We hear much of corporate power from the boardrooms. There is nc more dangerous concentration of corporate power than in the boardrooms of the large Crown corporations. Aii Canada is assiduously trying, through eyery means possible., tc wipe out its competitors. CNR management seem intent on wiping out their competitors and also a substantial portion of the trucking industry.
These are some of the main fears that I have about this bill. Does the CNR intend to reduce its railroading in the west? Does it intend to reduce its services to farmers in the grain handling industry which, after all, is the main reason for railroads in the west? Does it intend to move into the trucking field and establish a trucking monopoiy in that field and then attempt to have restrictive legislation passed so that the commercial life in the trucking field will be dominated by one large Crown corporation?
The movement of the CNR into the field for trucking means that it is attempting to get rid of one of its major competitors. In the riding I represent, the CNR Las bought out or.e of the more profitable truck lines, the Swan River-The Pas Transfer. This gives a partial monopoly on freight transportation to the
May 10, 1978

CNR and it is an object of some concern to many in the area. Transportation is certainly an area where it is difficult to have competition, but I think it is essentially wrong that the railway can smother its competition by buying out a trucking firm. Certainly it can afford to pay any price to obtain that trucking firm. There are no constraints so far as expenditures are concerned because, in the final analysis, the CNR has the backing of the treasury behind it.
Wherever possible we should preserve as many companies in the field as practical. That is why I certainly am concerned about the excursions of the CNR, taking over trucking firms and establishing what is a virtual monopoly in some areas. This has already occurred in the area I represent. It has not had a good response.
This bill allows CN to get out of railway passenger service, giving it to VIA Rail. We do know of course that rail passenger services in Canada as in all western countries, with the advent of the automobile have been much less popular, and have been a losing proposition so far as money is concerned. But all this bill does with the formation of VIA Rail is to transfer the deficit of rail passenger service on to VIA Rail. There is no evidence whatsoever that VIA Rail will be any more viable than under the present rail structure. As VIA Rail will still be using trains and passenger cars, the government will still have to meet VIA Rail's deficit.
One of the advantages of Bill C-17 is that it will eliminate the necessity of the federal treasury meeting the deficits of the CNR that rise from time to time. But the government can still guarantee CNR's loans from the private market. Like the Export Development Corporation's loans, all this does is that it allows the government to go on the note at the bank as a co-signer without the items actually appearing as a debit on the government's ledger. This is a deception of the worst order. Actually, borrowings that must be guaranteed by the federal treasury, either by the Export Development Corporation, the CNR, or other Crown corporations, should so appear on the ledger of the government.
I would like to speak briefly on the Churchill export movement and the necessity of the railways to upgrade the Churchill line to carry more grain. It represents Manitoba's alternate card that it can play, as well as other parts of the prairies, in attempting to get a better deal from eastern grain handling companies and installations. Depending on the circumstances, grain shipped through Thunder Bay averages about 25 cents a bushel less than shipped through the west coast. That is, it costs that much more.
Through a rather ingenious method of redistribution, shippers on the western half of the prairies pay some of this extra money received to shippers in the eastern half of the prairies. I think it is fair to say that the relative importance of western movements of grain will increase while the eastern movement through Thunder Bay will decrease in the foreseeable future. Indeed, if the laws of the markets prevail and if the true shipping costs were reflected, a much larger proportion of grain would go out through west coast ports and the dividing line would be considerably east of what it is now. But tradi-
Railway Act
tion, the earlier development of the Thunder Bay route and greater structures to handle grain on this traditional route have caused a reduced volume of west coast shipping that might have been expected to have happened. To the northeastern prairies and parkland regions of Manitoba and Saskatchewan, Churchill offers an alternative to prevent exorbitant tariff charges by eastern interests, and we have an example of this with the rise in tolls in the St. Lawrence Seaway. While the rise of tolls may be justified, still it has seriously compromised the income of western farmers.
Churchill lies on the ocean and, with a grain haul of 500 odd miles, it is as close as Thunder Bay is to the prairie grain region. It has been artificially constrained by government action and by port interests in Montreal and other eastern ports. This is a political fact of life and it is time that these constraints were removed. Greater use should be made of Churchill and, while it may have certain disadvantages, it has certain inherently great advantages. One is that with the weather being cold, grain can be stored indefinitely.
In conclusion, the port of Churchill is a logical grain shipping point for the future. A highway will eventually be built into Churchill. It will provide much of western Canada with an ocean port of a distance less than 500 miles away. If the CNR does not want to haul grain into Churchill, the trucks will.
